Amanda Chen
Daniel Martinez Hi, My strong point is usually hiking, and as for canyoneering, I haven't kept track of my rappels; I'm a beginner, maybe around 12 so far. 
In the last three weeks, my biggest challenges were in LSA and yesterday in Red Glare Gulch Canyon, where I did rappel number 3 (140-150 ft) and number 5 (190 ft).
Going to and paying for a school isn't within my means right now. For this reason, I'm really interested in continuing to learn wherever I have the opportunity. 
I saw that someone else here also asked about this, and I would be grateful if I could find a mentor; that would be great.
So, I'd like to know if it's possible for me to meet with you?
4w


Reply
Carlos Garcia
Amanda Chen I want you to know this is not a bad thing at all — you’ve been doing well out there, and I’ve seen your progress in the canyons we’ve run together.
One thing I do want to share honestly, as someone who cares about safety and learning: in canyoneering, the progression really matters. Before jumping into anchors and mentoring-level topics, it’s important to be very solid on rappel fundamentals — device use, lock-offs, contingencies, auto-backup techniques, and understanding what can go wrong on rappel and how to respond.
I’ve noticed sometimes you’re eager to move ahead quickly (like anchors), and that curiosity is great — but this is one of those activities where going step-by-step is key. Strong rappel skills first, then anchors later. Rushing that order can actually hold you back instead of helping.
We’re always happy to share knowledge and practice with you, and we are teaching as we go — but structured classes can really help fill in gaps and give you a solid foundation faster and safer. It’s not a negative at all; it’s actually a smart move.
Just wanted to share this with you respectfully and honestly. You’re welcome with us, and the goal is always learning safely and building skills the right way. Let’s just take it one step at a time.
4w

Rachel Marie Stone
Definitely recommend running a canyon to make sure you’re stoked (you totally will be), but I highly agree with others about taking a course. 
The course will teach you the minimum skills to contribute and generally be safe in a canyon. Mentors are great too, but different people have different risk tolerances. I think it’s important to have a base foundation and healthy skepticism before seeking continued mentorship/trusting a single person/friend to teach you. 
The Uber Adventures classes and rendezvous are awesome. That’s how I found all of my early and closest canyon friends

Training is great, mentorship is great, you’ll progress fastest if you can secure both.
Take a course, find an experienced leader whose style you like, and you get along with, and start running with them. Ask them questions, help them out, try to contribute to team safety and efficient progression. Listen to your mentor even when you don’t want to hear it.
Good luck have fun be safe
